newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.

text.p: SHIPS BOUND FOR INDONESIA DELAYED BY PROTEST
The Maritime Union's campaign targeting cargo vessels bound for Indonesia to protest against the country's human rights record has hit the Port of Newcastle again.
The Dutch owned ship, Palmgracht was due to sail out of Newcastle today, loaded with steel, bound for Indonesia.
But the Maritime Union has placed a 24 hour ban on the vessel, as part of its protest against Indonesia's human rights record, and the jailing of a number of the country's trade union leaders.

Newcastle union organiser, Jim Boyle, says the bans have been imposed over the past few months, and although the Australian and Indonesian Governments have condemned the action, there has been a good reaction from the wider community.
SURVEY FINDS NEARLY 80% APPROVE OF VOLUNTARY EUTHANASIA
A University of Queensland survey has found 79 per cent of Northern Territorians approve of voluntary euthanasia.
Researcher, Colleen Cartwright, says the response partly reflects respondents' personal experiences with sick family members.

Ms Cartwright says most of those surveyed believed that ahead of pain, important considerations were the loss of control, dignity and independence felt by terminally ill people. She says some people may see euthanasia as a way of taking back control.
The survey also found only 35 per cent of Territory doctors agree with the law.

Ms Cartwright admits the survey's unrepresentative because of difficulties in getting the views of people in remote areas. The survey will be presented to the Senate Committee inquiring into the legislation.
GERMAN LEADER TO VISIT FAR NORTH QUEENSLAND
Word about far north Queensland's charm seems to be spreading among world leaders.
U-S President, Bill Clinton's visit to Port Douglas received worldwide coverage late last year, and now German Chancellor, Helmut Kohl, is to follow suit.
Chancellor Kohl will visit in May, staying at the same resort as the Clintons.
Steve Noakes, from the local Promotion Bureau, says the German leader will meet major Australian political and business leaders during his overnight stay.
Mr Noakes says the visit is another coup for far north Queensland.
WALLIS LAKE OYSTER GROWERS FEEL LEFT IN THE DARK

In northern New South Wales, Wallis Lake oyster growers have spoken out against the Health Department for not telling them of the death last week of a man who contracted Hepatitis A from local oysters.
Industry spokeswoman, Kerry Jackson, from the Department of Fisheries, says she heard of the death through the media yesterday, and is disappointed growers weren't told first.
Dr Jackson says the industry has bent over backwards to protect the public since the outbreak, and is funding some of the research into the source itself.
She says growers have been hit hard enough without the added trauma of being kept in the dark by the Department of Health.
APPEAL LODGED FOR LONGER SENTENCE FOR BOND
An appeal's been lodged in Western Australia's Supreme Court against the four year jail term imposed on Alan Bond for corporate fraud.
The prosecution had sought a jail term of around ten years.
It argued Bond's offences were among the worst of their kind, involving the transfer of hundreds of millions of dollars between companies to the detriment of many minor shareholders.
The Commonwealth Director of Public Prosecutions lodged the appeal arguing for a longer sentence.
Bond is currently serving a prison term for other fraud offences.
